Decoupling local classicality from classical explainability: A noncontextual model for bilocal classical theory and a locally-classical but contextual theory
Sina Soltani, Marco Erba, David Schmid, John H. Selby

Abstract
We construct an ontological model for the theory known as bilocal classical theory [ 21 ] . To our knowledge, this is only the second time that an ontological model has been constructed for an entire theory, rather than just for some particular scenarios within a theory. This result refutes a conjecture from Ref. [ 21 ] which suggested that there might be no local-realist ontological model for bilocal classical theory. Moreover, it is the first time that an ontological model has been constructed for a theory that fails to be locally tomographic, showing that the assumption of local tomography underpinning the structure theorem in Ref. [ 62 ] is a genuine limitation of the theorem. This demonstrates that in general there is no tension between failures of local tomography and classical explainability (i.e., generalised noncontextuality). In fact, bilocal classical theory is in many ways more simply understood via the underlying ontological model than it is within its original formulation (much as how odd-dimensional stabiliser subtheories can be more simply understood via Spekkens’ toy theory). Furthermore, this result naturally leads to the question, does every locally-classical theory admit of an ontological model? By constructing a concrete counterexample, we show that this is not the case. Our findings demonstrate that there is no straightforward relationship between theories being locally-classical, and them being classically-explainable. This shows that the fundamental status of compositional properties (such as local tomography) is not a technical side-issue, but a central and unavoidable question for a coherent understanding even of classicality itself.



1
Introduction

The formalism of operational probabilistic theories (OPTs)
[
14
,
19
,
57
,
73
,
22
]
(closely related to the one of generalised probabilistic theories, or GPTs for short
[
5
,
34
,
33
,
44
,
54
]
) is a broad framework encompassing essentially all theories that admit of an operational characterisation. In this framework, classical probability theory (CT) has traditionally been singled out as the unique “classical” theory
[
5
,
34
,
33
,
81
,
54
,
2
,
67
]
. From an operational standpoint, this conception of classicality essentially boils down to three characteristic traits of systems in CT:
joint perfect discriminability of pure states
—implying that every state space is geometrically described by a simplex; the
distinguishability of any two bipartite states by using the statistics of measurements on the individual components
—entailing, for simplicial systems, a composition rule that can be described by the Cartesian product; and that
all mathematically consistent processes are physically possible
(“everything that is not forbidden is allowed”
[
19
]
). The second feature operationally boils down to the
local tomography

[
82
,
31
,
12
,
47
]
or
local discriminability

[
19
]
principles, while the third is known as the
no-restriction hypothesis

[
14
,
34
]
, which are important properties also satisfied by quantum theory. Note that
joint perfect discriminability of pure states
is a single-system property, while
local tomography
is a multi-system, compositional notion.
In brief, CT is the operational probabilistic theory that contains all and only processes consistent with simpliciality and local tomography.

One can also ask which theories are
classically-explainable
, in the sense that they can be reasonably explained by CT. This question was first answered in Refs.
[
65
,
62
,
64
,
53
]
, which argued that one GPT can explain the statistical, convex, and compositional structures of another if and only if there is a linear and diagram preserving map between the two. In particular, then, a GPT is classically-explainable if it can be
embedded
into CT in this manner. Such an embedding is called an ontological model of a GPT. This conception of classical explainability was subsequently explored in a number of works
[
68
,
70
,
73
,
63
,
59
]
.

This notion of classical explainability coincides with the existence of a generalised-noncontextual
[
74
]
explanation (for the operational theory which leads to the GPT
[
62
]
) within an ontological model
[
32
]
. The latter approach can also be motivated by a methodological version of Leibniz’s principle
[
77
]
, by its equivalence to the existence of some positive quasiprobabilistic representation
[
76
,
62
]
, and by its equivalence to the above notion of classical explainability. Failures of generalised noncontextuality are strong manifestations of failures of classical explainability, and have been found (and often leveraged as resources) in the realms of quantum computation
[
61
,
71
]
, state discrimination
[
66
,
26
,
52
,
72
]
, interference
[
10
,
11
,
9
,
28
]
, compatibility
[
69
,
68
,
23
,
78
]
, uncertainty relations
[
8
]
, metrology
[
50
]
, thermodynamics
[
50
,
17
,
49
]
, weak values
[
55
,
37
]
, coherence
[
58
,
80
,
79
]
, quantum Darwinism
[
3
]
, information processing and communication
[
75
,
13
,
1
,
60
,
84
,
30
,
27
]
, cloning
[
48
]
, broadcasting
[
35
]
, pre- and post-selection paradoxes
[
46
]
, randomness certification
[
56
]
, psi-epistemicity
[
45
]
, and Bell
[
83
,
64
]
and Kochen-Specker scenarios
[
38
,
39
,
41
,
42
,
43
,
40
,
29
]
.

Relatedly, some recent works
[
20
,
21
,
23
,
57
]
on OPTs have explored the idea, and modifications thereof, of
locally-classical
theories—that is, those theories where all systems are classical in the strict sense of CT (i.e., containing all and only processes consistent with simpliciality), while the system-composition rule may differ from that of standard CT (thus generally violating local tomography)
[
20
,
21
,
24
,
12
]
.
1
1

1

Note that, since our approach is
compositional
, composite systems can be always taken to be themselves components of larger composites. Motivated by this observation, “locally-classical” here means that every system, be it elementary or composite, is classical—while, globally, the theory may differ from the standard classical theory, particularly in its composition rule. Such a terminology therefore slightly differs from the one used, e.g., in Refs.
[
4
,
18
]
, where the analysis was carried out for multipartite correlation scenarios and, accordingly, “locally quantum” refers to settings where the elementary components are quantum, while the global systems need not necessarily be quantum.
Such theories can only differ from CT in their composition rule, which may not obey local tomography. The first example of a fully-fledged locally-classical theory that violates local tomography is known as
bilocal classical theory

[
21
]
, which we introduce in Sec.
1.3
.

In this paper, we further explore the connections between these different concepts relating to classicality, that is, between
local classicality
and
classical explainability
(in the precise senses described above). Our first result is to show that bilocal classical theory is classically-explainable. Hence, modifications to the composition rule of classical theory (as an OPT) are not necessarily incompatible with the existence of an underlying ontology which composes following the standard “classical” composition rule (the Cartesian product). On the other hand, we construct alternative examples of locally-classical theories (following the construction of
latent theories
introduced in Ref.
[
24
]
) which we prove are
not
classically-explainable. Consequently, locally-classical theories that fail to be tomographically local are
sometimes, but not always,
classically-explainable. An important direction for future work would be to find some way to classify such theories, for example, by finding some physical principle which singles out which are classically-explainable.

In the first part of this paper, we begin with a concise overview of the framework of operational probabilistic theories, tailored to the needs of our discussion. We then turn to the two specific OPTs that play a central role in our work:
classical theory
and
bilocal classical theory
. We then define the concept of a map between (the transformations of) two OPTs, and as a special case,
ontological models
of OPTs
[
73
]
, concluding the section by defining what it means for such a model to be
classically-explainable
. In the second part of the paper, we construct such a model for bilocal classical theory and show that the constructed model is a consistent one. Finally, we conclude the paper with a no-go theorem concerning another type of locally-classical theories, termed
latent classical theories
, for which we prove that no ontological model can be constructed.

1.1
Operational probabilistic theories

In this section, we briefly review the framework of operational probabilistic theories (OPTs).
2
2

2

Or, more precisely, the framework of operational probabilistic theories which satisfy
process tomography
, i.e., those OPTs that have been quotiented
[
73
]
relative to the operational equivalence relation induced by (
17
) below.
For a more comprehensive review we refer readers to
[
19
]
and the forthcoming work
[
22
]
. The primitives in the OPT framework are systems, transformations, instruments, and probabilities. A system is representative of a physical object under study in a laboratory, such as a particle, atom, or field. A transformation describes the evolution a system undergoes, while an instrument specifies the set of possible transformations that may occur in a given probabilistic process. The OPT framework prescribes the probabilities of different outcomes one would obtain in a measurement, given the preparations and evolutions that have occurred before the measurement, taking into account how these primitives are composed.

We denote the class of systems for a generic OPT
\Theta
as
\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
. For single systems, we use Latin characters
A,B,C,\cdots\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
. We denote the class of transformations
from system
A
to
B
as
\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
, and we depict a transformation

t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
as

T^{A\to B}_{X}=[t_{x}]_{x\in X};\;\;\;\forall x\in X,\;\;t_{x}\in\textbf{Transf}(A\rightarrow B).

(4)

Furthermore, since an identity transformation represents doing nothing to systems, we demand for an identity
transformation to satisfy

I_{B}\circ t_{x}=t_{x}=t_{x}\circ I_{A},\;\;\;\forall t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B).

(7)

When not describing any physical system, we use the trivial system
I\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
, which satisfies
IA=A=AI
for all
A\in

Sys
(
\Theta
). Since composing
I
with any system is equivalent to doing nothing, we represent it as a blank space. Thus, for a particular class of transformations

\rho\in\textbf{Transf}(I\to A)
and
a\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to I)
, we can depict them as

(8)

These are respectively called
states
and
effects
. Sometimes, we denote a state for a system
A
as
|\rho)_{A}
, and an effect
a
as
(a|_{A}
. We also denote the sequential composition of a state
|\rho)_{A}
and an effect
(a|_{A}
as
(a|\rho)_{A}
.

To describe the exchange of systems, an OPT requires the notion of swapping, that is, a family
\sigma
of invertible transformations
such that, for any two systems
A
and
B
, their exchange is represented by
\sigma_{A,B}
, depicted as

(12)

Note that the compositional structure of an OPT, as described here, corresponds to the structure of a braided monoidal category. A key feature of the OPT framework is that the primal objects are the instruments. In this formulation, the category of transformations
is defined as being induced by the category of instruments
rather than the other way around. However, for our purposes, we are primarily interested in transformations
rather than instruments,
and we do not explore the full implications of treating instruments
as primal. This is because our goal is to construct, or show the nonexistence of, an ontological model for specific OPTs, and Ref.
[
73
]
showed that, for the OPTs of our interest, the instrument structure can be disregarded. Based on this result, our focus in this section is primarily on transformations.

In the OPT framework, a transformation
\lambda
with both trivial input and output is called a
scalar
, which we depict as

(14)

This probability
p
is the chance that
\rho
occurs among all other states in its corresponding state instrument,
t
among all transformations in its instrument, and
a
among all outcomes in its corresponding effect instrument. The assignment thus defines a probability distribution over all transformations in the respective instruments.
We define parallel composition of scalars as

p\boxtimes q:=pq,\;\;\;\forall p,q\in\textbf{Transf}(I\to I),

(15)

which is simply the multiplication of real numbers. We can also define
multiplication by scalars
, that is, for every
p\in\textbf{Transf}(I\to I)
and every
t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
, one has

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}

(17)

for every
E\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
, every state
\rho\in\textbf{Transf}(I\to AE)
, and every effect
a\in\textbf{Transf}(BE\to I)
. Note that in the full framework of OPTs this is in fact only required to be an equivalence relation rather than an equality, however, one can always quotient with respect to this relation and obtain an OPT of the sort we have defined here.

Note that in an OPT, as can be seen from (
17
),
\textbf{St}(A):=\textbf{Transf}(I\to A)
can be identified with a set of functionals from
\textbf{Eff}(A):=\textbf{Transf}(A\to I)
to the real interval
\left[0,1\right]
, and vice versa. Moreover, the set of states separates the set of effects, and the set of effects separates the set of states. This means that for any pair of distinct states
|\rho)_{A},|\sigma)_{A}\in\textbf{St}(A)
, there exists an effect
(a|_{A}\in\textbf{Eff}(A)
such that
(a|\rho)_{A}\neq(a|\sigma)_{A}
(and similarly for any pair of different effects). It is well known
[
14
,
16
,
15
,
19
]
that these two properties give rise to a linear structure, that is, one can define a complete class of linearly independent vectors in
\textbf{St}(A)
that span a real vector space, denoted by
\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(A):=\text{Span}_{\mathbb{R}}\;\textbf{St}(A)
. Similarly, the space
\textbf{Eff}(A)
spans, in general, a subspace of its dual vector space, defined as
\textbf{Eff}_{\mathbb{R}}(A):=\text{Span}_{\mathbb{R}}\;\textbf{Eff}(A)\subseteq\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(A)^{*}
. The dimension of the system
A
is then given by
D_{A}:=\text{dim}\;\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(A)
. In this work, we only consider finite-dimensional OPTs, for which the equalities
\textbf{Eff}_{\mathbb{R}}(A)=\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(A)^{*}
and
\text{dim}\;\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(A)=\text{dim}\;\textbf{Eff}_{\mathbb{R}}(A)
holds for every system
A
.

Analogous to states and effects, one can associate a real vector space to transformations as well. Specifically, transformations from
A
to
B
can be viewed as functionals that take a state-effect pair and assign a probability. As such, they belong to a vector space, which allows us to define
\textbf{Transf}_{\mathbb{R}}(A\to B):=\text{Span}_{\mathbb{R}}\,\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
. In the OPT framework, the set of transformations from system
A
to system
B
forms a convex and bounded subset of the real vector space
\textbf{Transf}_{\mathbb{R}}(A\to B)
.

As a consequence of (
17
), any transformation
t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
naturally gives rise to a linear map
\hat{t}_{E}
from
\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(AE)
to
\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(BE)
for every system
E
. Thus, each transformation
t
is fully specified by the collection of such linear maps
\{\hat{t}_{E}\}_{E\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)}
. In particular, two transformations
t_{1}
and
t_{2}
from
A
to
B
are equal if and only if

t_{1}=t_{2}\iff\hat{t}_{1,E}=\hat{t}_{2,E},\quad\forall E\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta).

(18)

In general, the full infinite family
\{\hat{t}_{E}\}_{E\in\text{Sys}(\Theta)}
over all systems
E
may be needed to completely determine a transformation. However, in some cases, this is not required. For instance, in “locally tomographic” theories which we will explain, each transformation is uniquely determined by its action on the system alone, meaning the map with trivial ancilla
E
suffices.

An agent may choose to conflate outcomes within any subset of a instrument’s outcome space, that is, ignore distinctions between transformations in that subset. To formalise this in the OPT framework, we define coarse-graining for an instrument
T^{A\to B}_{X}=[t_{x}]_{x\in X}
and any subset
Y\subseteq X
as

t_{Y}:=\sum_{y\in Y}t_{y},

(19)

where both sequential and parallel composition distribute over summation. We can also consider
refinement
for a transformation
t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
, that is a set
\{t_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}
such that
t=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}t_{i}
. Likewise, we can define
convex refinement
of
t
, that is defined as a set
\{t_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}
, such that one has
t=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}p_{i}t_{i}
, for some probability distribution
\{p_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}}
. A transformation
t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
is called
atomic
if, whenever one has the refinement
t=t_{1}+t_{2}
for some
t_{1},t_{2}\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
, it follows that
t_{1}\propto t_{2}
. That is, atomic transformations are those that, up to a scalar factor, cannot be further refined into other transformations. An analogous notion applies to convex refinements: a transformation
t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
is called
extremal
if, for any
t_{1},t_{2}\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
and
p\in(0,1)
, the convex refinement
t=pt_{1}+(1-p)t_{2}
implies
t_{1}=t_{2}
. In other words, extremal transformations only admit trivial convex refinements.

A transformation
t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
is called
deterministic
if there exists a singleton instrument such that
T_{\star}=\{t\}
. This means the transformation occurs with certainty, having a marginal probability of 1. Consequently, since singleton instruments correspond to deterministic transformations, for any instrument
T_{X}^{A\to B}=\{t_{x}\}_{x\in X}\in\textbf{Instr}(A\to B)
, the full coarse-graining, i.e.,
t_{X}=\sum_{x\in X}t_{x}
, is a deterministic transformation. Deterministic transformations are referred to as
channels
, while deterministic extremal states are known as
pure states
. A transformation
\mathscr{R}\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
is called
reversible
, if there exists a transformation
\mathscr{R}^{-1}\in\textbf{Sys}(A\to B)
such that
\mathscr{R}^{-1}\mathscr{R}=\mathcal{I}_{A}
and
\mathscr{R}\mathscr{R}^{-1}=\mathcal{I}_{B}
. To account for zero probabilities within the framework, we assume
0\in\textbf{Transf}(I\to I)
. From scalar multiplication (
16
), it follows that for any
t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
and any systems
A,B\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
, one can define a
null
transformation
\varepsilon_{A\to B}:=0\cdot t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
. This null transformation satisfies the condition that for all
E\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
,

(20)

An OPT is said to satisfy
local tomography
, if and only if, for any two distinct bipartite state
\rho\in\textbf{St}(AB)
and
\rho^{\prime}\in\textbf{St}(AB)
, there exist a product effect
a_{1}\boxtimes a_{2}\in\textbf{Eff}(AB)
, where
a_{1}\in\textbf{Eff}(A)
and
a_{2}\in\textbf{Eff}(B)
, such that

(21)

In other words, two bipartite states can be distinguished solely through local measurements. In a locally tomographic OPT, the complete specification of any state is achievable using only the statistics of local measurements. That is, two states are identical if they yield the same statistics for all local measurements. An OPT
\Theta
is locally tomographic if and only if the dimension condition
D_{AB}=D_{A}D_{B}
holds for all systems
A,B\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)

[
19
]
. Under this condition, for each composite system
AB
, the real vector space
\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(AB)
is spanned by product states, and moreover, to fully determine a transformation
t\in\textbf{Transf}(A\to B)
via (
17
), it suffices to examine its action on the system alone, using only the trivial system as the ancilla.

The notion of local tomography can be generalised to
n
-local tomography

[
21
,
31
]
, wherein a theory exhibits
n
-local tomography if the state of a composite system can be completely determined using measurement statistics from subsystems of up to
n
components—that is, from
1
-component,
2
-component, …, up to
n
-component measurements. Equivalently,
n
-local tomography means that for any
n\leq m
, the set of effects formed by conical combinations of parallel compositions
a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{l}
, where
a_{j}
is
k_{j}
-partite with
k_{j}\leq n
for each
j
, is sufficient to distinguish (i.e., is separating for) all
m
-partite states. For the special case
n=2
, the theory is referred to as a
bilocally tomographic
theory. In such a theory, both local and bipartite measurements—as well as conical combinations of their parallel compositions—are required to fully characterise a composite state. We will review one of those theories in the subsequent sections, known as bilocal classical theory.

The condition that the probability distribution associated with a preparation instrument does not depend on the specific choice of observation instrument applied at its output is commonly referred to as
causality
. It is well known that this notion of
causality is equivalent to the principle of no-signalling from future and equivalent to the statement that each system possesses a
unique deterministic effect

[
19
]
. In particular, an OPT is said to be causal if and only if every system
A
admits a unique deterministic effect, represented as

(23)

where for the deterministic states, this condition reduces to normalisation condition.

In the OPT framework, one may also consider
conditional instruments

[
14
]
, where the selection of an instrument depends on the outcome of a previously performed instrument. That is, based on the result of one instrument—i.e., an element of the outcome space—a subsequent instrument, conditioned on that outcome, is applied in sequence. This notion enables the definition of a stricter form of causality, known as
strong causality
. An OPT is said to be strongly causal if every conditional instrument is itself an instrument of the theory. In other words, implementing a conditional instrument must result in a valid instrument within the theory. The reason this property is referred to as strong causality is that, in any OPT satisfying it, the ability to implement arbitrary conditional instruments implies the uniqueness of the deterministic effect for every system—i.e., standard causality. Hence, causality is a necessary condition for strong causality. However, the converse does not necessarily hold.

In this paper, we do not attempt to formalise the notion of strong causality, as its technical details are not directly relevant to our purposes. What is essential for our discussion is the result presented in Ref.
[
73
]
, which shows that in a strongly causal OPT, the construction of an ontological model—discussed in the following subsection—can proceed without reference to the instrument structure of the OPT framework. Instead, one may focus exclusively on the structure of transformations. This insight supports our earlier remark in this section: although the instrument structure is one of the primitives of the OPT framework, our analysis will primarily focus on transformations. This is because our ultimate goal is to construct an ontological model for bilocal classical theory, which is strongly causal. Therefore, the results of Ref.
[
73
]
are directly applicable to our study here.

Finally, it is intended that the concrete models of OPTs presented in the following all satisfy the property of
existence and uniqueness of system-decomposition

[
57
, §6, Def. 14]
, that is: every system can be
uniquely
decomposed as a parallel composition of non-trivial elementary systems. This property, which was already exploited for the construction of
latent theories
in Ref.
[
24
]
, allows for the concrete definition of parallel composition rules by specifying the least number of equalities between different decompositions of arbitrary systems. More specifically, one may start by defining all of the elementary systems for a theory, so that the composite ones are defined by strings on the alphabet of the elementary ones. For instance, finite-dimensional quantum theory may be defined by setting qudits
Q_{d}
, for every integer
d\geq 2
, to be the (non-trivial) elementary quantum systems; thus, instead of strict equalities, one generally has just isomorphisms of the kind

Q_{l}\otimes Q_{m}\cong Q_{m}\otimes Q_{l},\quad Q_{l}\otimes Q_{m}\cong Q_{lm},\quad Q_{l}\otimes Q_{mn}\cong Q_{m}\otimes Q_{ln}.

Accordingly, it will be sufficient to specify the elementary systems of an OPT together with a parallel composition rule for them: arbitrary systems will be then given by the monoid that is freely generated by
the elementary systems. From a category-theoretic viewpoint, an OPT satisfying unique system-decomposition is a
coloured PROP

[
51
,
7
]
.

1.2
Classical theory

Classical theory is a strongly causal OPT
\Delta
in which the pure states of every system
A\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
, together with the null state
|\varepsilon)_{\text{A}}
, constitute the vertices of a
D_{A}
-simplex. A
D_{A}
-simplex is the convex hull of
D_{A}+1
affinely independent points, where every every state
\rho\in\textbf{St}(A)
has a unique subconvex decomposition into pure states. In classical theory, the pure states of each system are jointly perfectly discriminable. A set of deterministic (i.e., normalised) states
\{|\rho_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}
for a system
A
is said to be jointly perfectly discriminable if there exists an observation instrument
\{(a_{i}|_{\text{A}}\}_{i=1}^{n}
such that

\left(a_{i}|\rho_{i^{{}^{\prime}}}\right)=\delta_{i,i^{{}^{\prime}}},\;\;\;\forall i,i^{{}^{\prime}}\in\{1,2,\ldots,n\}.

(24)

In classical theory, systems are represented by finite-dimensional Euclidean vector spaces
\mathbb{R}^{D_{A}}
, where
D_{A}
denotes the dimension of system
A
. For a composite system
AB
, the dimension is given by
D_{AB}=D_{A}D_{B}
, meaning that the composite system is represented by the Euclidean vector space
\mathbb{R}^{D_{A}D_{B}}
. This dimensional relationship ensures that classical theory satisfies the principle of local tomography. Moreover, for a composite system
AB
, the pure states form the vertices of a
D_{A}D_{B}
-simplex and are precisely the product states of pure states from systems
A
and
B
.

Transformations from system
A
to system
B
are represented by substochastic matrices
M\in\textbf{SubStoch}(A\to B)
, while deterministic transformations correspond to stochastic matrices
S\in\textbf{Stoch}(A\to B)
. As a special case, states are (subnormalised) probability distributions, effects correspond to response functions, and scalars correspond to probabilities. Sequential composition is given by the composition of (sub)stochastic matrices, whereas parallel composition is given by the usual tensor product. Instruments in classical theory are those where the full coarse graining gives a deterministic transformations, i.e., a stochastic matrix.

From this point onward, instead of using uppercase Latin characters, we represent systems in classical theory by an integer
n
, which denotes the dimension of the system. In particular, the trivial system is represented by
n=1
. Additionally, we depict systems in classical theory using grey wires

where for lower indices, one has

1\leq i_{1}\leq n_{1}
,
1\leq i_{2}\leq n_{2}
,
\ldots
,
1\leq i_{p}\leq n_{p}
, and for upper indices, one has

1\leq l_{1}\leq m_{1}
,
1\leq l_{2}\leq m_{2}
,
\ldots
,
1\leq l_{q}\leq m_{q}
, and,
\lambda\in[0,1]
. In classical theory, sequential or parallel composition of atomic transformations yields another atomic transformation.

We call atomic transformations with
\lambda=1

normalised atomic transformations
which we denote as
\mathscr{A}_{i_{0}}^{l}
. Every arbitrary transformation
t
in classical theory, from a system
n
to
m
, can be written as the unique conical combination of normalised atomic transformations, that is

denotes a permutation of the

elements.

Note that, since classical theory satisfies local tomography, there is no need to include ancillary systems in order to fully characterise transformations. Consequently, atomic and reversible transformations can be described as specific instances of general transformations without reference to any ancillary system, as we have done in this analysis.

1.3
Bilocal classical theory

Bilocal classical theory (BCT) was first introduced in
[
21
]
as a consistent theory of locally-classical systems with a composition rule that differs from that of classical theory–but in such a way that the state and effect spaces of composite systems are also classical (identical to that of the simplicial theory). Despite the fact that all systems are themselves classical, the exotic composition rule in BCT leads it to exhibit several features absent in classical theory, such as entanglement, cloning, entanglement swapping, dense coding, additivity of classical capacities, non-monogamous entanglement, and hypersignaling. In this section, we briefly review the basic properties of BCT that are most relevant to our purposes. In the following sections, we aim to construct an ontological model for BCT. To that end, we will focus in particular on the composition rule, the characterisation of pure states and pure effects, and atomic transformations in BCT. We do not aim to prove all of the properties we mention here. Interested readers can find full proofs and more discussions in Ref.
[
21
]
.

Bilocal classical theory (BCT) is a strongly causal OPT, in which every system is classical—that is, each system is described by a finite-dimensional OPT whose pure states are the vertices of a simplex and are jointly perfectly discriminable. Similar to classical theory, for a system
A
, every state
\rho\in\textbf{St}(A)
has a unique subconvex decomposition into pure states. We represent each single system by an integer
n
that denotes its dimension, which for the trivial system, one has
n=1
. The main difference from classical theory lies in the composition rule. For any two single systems with dimensions
n
and
m
, the dimension of the composite system, denoted as
D(n,m)
, is given by

D(n,m)=D(m,n)=\begin{cases}2nm,&\text{if }n\neq 1\neq m,\\
n,&\text{if }m=1.\end{cases}

(35)

Hence, we represent a composite bipartite system
n\boxtimes m
, formed from subsystems
n
and
m
, as
2nm
. For this system, pure states are given as the vertices of a
2nm
-simplex. In light of the composition rule, BCT does not exhibit local tomography; instead, it exhibits bilocal tomography, which is the reason it has been named as bilocal classical theory.
We represent a system
n
in BCT pictorially as as thick violet wire

\hbox to58.01pt{\vbox to9.82pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 29.00276pt\lower-0.55pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \hbox to0.0pt{
{
{}{}{}}{}{{}}{}{

(39)

This composition rule for pure states implies that when two pure states are composed in parallel, the resulting state—unlike in classical theory—is no longer pure. However, despite this difference, composite systems in BCT remain classical systems. Consequently, every state in BCT can still be expressed as a unique subconvex combination of pure states.

where for lower indices, one has

1\leq i_{1}\leq n_{1}
,
1\leq i_{2}\leq n_{2}
,
\ldots
,
1\leq i_{p}\leq n_{p}
,
and
s_{1}
,
s_{2}
,
\ldots
,
s_{p-1}\in\{0,1\}
,
and for upper indices, one has

1\leq l_{1}\leq m_{1}
,
1\leq l_{2}\leq m_{2}
,
\ldots
,
1\leq l_{q}\leq m_{q}
,
and
t_{1}
,
t_{2}
,
\ldots
,
t_{q-1}\in\{0,1\}
.
Also, one has
\lambda\in[0,1]
and
\tau\in\{0,1\}
. More details on how to characterise atomic transformations on composite systems can be found in App.
B
.

for all systems
n
,
o
, and
m
, all
1\leq i_{0}\leq n
,
1\leq l\leq o
,
1\leq i^{\prime}_{0}\leq o
,
1\leq l^{\prime}\leq m
, all
\tau,\tau^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}
, and for all
\lambda,\lambda^{\prime}\in[0,1]
, where
\tilde{\tau}:=\tau\oplus\tau^{\prime}
and
\tilde{\lambda}:=\delta_{l,i^{\prime}_{0}}\lambda\lambda^{\prime}
. In the case of
m=1
, the corresponding effect on the right-hand side will also be an atomic effect. Using (
53
), It can also be shown that the sequential composition of atomic transformations on composite systems results in another atomic transformation. However, in the case of parallel composition, there is a stark contrast between BCT and classical theory. When atomic transformations are composed in parallel, the resulting transformation is no longer atomic. The same holds for the parallel composition of atomic effects, where the resulting effect is no longer atomic.

For every non-trivial system
n\neq 1
, and every system
m
, every arbitrary transformation
t
in BCT, from system
n
to
m
, can be written as a conical combination of atomic transformations from system
n
to
m

\displaystyle=\sum_{i_{0},l,\tau}a(i_{0},l,\tau)\delta_{i_{0},i^{\prime}_{0}}\delta_{l,l^{\prime}}\delta_{\tau,\tau^{\prime}}=a(i^{\prime}_{0},l^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})=0\;,

(62)

where by appropriate choice of
\rho
and
a
, we can show that all the coefficients
a(i_{0},l,\tau)
, for every
i_{0}
,
l
, and
\tau
, are zero as well. This concludes the proof as it implies that
C(i_{0},l,\tau)=C^{\prime}(i_{0},l,\tau)
. Therefore, all possible conical combinations of normalised atomic transformations for an arbitrary transformation
t
in (
57
) are equal, and hence, every arbitrary transformation can be expressed as a unique conical combination of normalised atomic transformations.

(63)

for every
1\leq i\leq n
,
1\leq j\leq m
,
1\leq k\leq n_{E}
, and every
s,t\in\{0,1\}
. Swapping in BCT satisfies
\sigma_{n,m}^{-1}=\sigma_{m,n}
for every system
m
and
n
. Hence, BCT is symmetric.

Note that, since BCT does not satisfy local tomography, it is necessary to consider ancillary systems
E
in order to fully characterise transformations—unlike classical theory, where, as we have seen, atomic and reversible transformations can be fully characterised without ancillary systems. In BCT, however, such characterisations require the inclusion of ancillary systems, as we have undertaken in our analysis. As a category, BCT is consistent in the sense that it satisfies the required coherence conditions. Moreover, as an OPT, it exhibits a consistent probabilistic structure. These properties have been discussed and demonstrated in Ref.
[
21
]
. We have also included a very brief introduction to
reversible
transformations of BCT in App.
D.1
.

1.4
Ontological models and classical explainability

1.4.1
Maps between different OPTs

In this section, we first introduce the general notion of a map between transformations of two operational probabilistic theories (OPTs), and then focus on specific types of such maps as introduced in
[
73
]
. For the purposes of this paper, we adapt those definitions—without loss of generality—to suit our context.

Definition 1.2

(Maps between two OPTs)
.

A map between two OPTs
\phi:\Theta\rightarrow\Phi
, takes every system
\text{A}\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
to a system
\phi(\text{A})\in\textbf{Sys}(\Phi)
and maps every transformation
t
of
\Theta
to a transformation
\phi{(t)}
of
\Phi
, depicted as

(64)

where for the trivial system, one has
\phi(I)=I
.

A map
\phi
is said to be
linear
if for every
r_{x}\in\mathbb{R}
, every system
A
and
B\in\textbf{Sys}(\Theta)
, and every transformation
t_{x}\in\textbf{Transf}(A\rightarrow B)
, such that
\sum_{x}r_{x}t_{x}\in\textbf{Transf}(A\rightarrow B)
, one has

\phi{\left(\sum_{x}r_{x}t_{x}\right)}=\sum_{x}r_{x}\phi{\left(t_{x}\right)}.

(65)

every two arbitrary transformation
t_{1}
and
t_{2}
Note that this definition implies that a map
\phi
, takes every state in
\Theta
to a state in
\Phi
, every effect in
\Theta
to an effect in
\Phi
, and every scalar in
\Phi
to a scalar in
\Theta
. This definition also implies that every instrument
\Theta
is mapped to an instrument in
\Phi
, where each transformation of the instrument in
\Phi
, is simply given by the action of the map on the corresponding transformation in
\Theta
.

A map is said to be
diagram-preserving

\phi_{\text{\tiny DP}}:\Theta\rightarrow\Phi
if composing transformations before or after applying the map remains equivalent. For example,

\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}\;\;,

(69)

is a linear map from a strongly causal OPT
\Theta
to classical theory
\Delta
that satisfies diagram preservation, probability preservation, and maps every instrument in
\Theta
to a valid instrument in
\Delta
.

An ontological model for a strongly causal OPT associates each transformation with a substochastic transformation in classical theory. Additionally, it assigns a classical state to every state and a classical effect to every effect. Each system
A
in the OPT is mapped to a classical system whose dimension, denoted by
\Lambda_{A}
, specifies the size of the corresponding ontic space
[
32
]
.

Note that in defining the general notion of a map between two OPTs, we focus solely on how it assigns a transformation from one OPT to a transformation in another. However, one could argue that since the OPT framework includes instrument
structure, maps between OPTs, including ontological models, could alternatively be defined in terms of how they map instruments rather than transformations. Nevertheless, it has been shown in
[
73
]
that for OPTs that are strongly causal—including BCT—the instrument structure can be disregarded when one aims to construct ontological models, and ontological models can be fully defined at the level of transformations, which aligns with the definition we adopt here. This is precisely why strong causality is required in our definition of ontological models.

Thus, constructing an ontological model for a given strongly causal OPT requires specifying only how the model acts on the transformations of the theory, not on the instruments. If the constructed model is consistent and qualifies as a valid ontological model, then, as explained in
[
62
,
73
]
, it confirms that the OPT of interest is classically-explainable and compatible with the notion of generalised noncontextuality. In the following sections, we carry out this construction for BCT, focusing in particular on how the model maps systems, pure states, pure effects, and normalised atomic transformations. We then demonstrate the model’s consistency, thereby confirming the existence of an ontological model for BCT, and thus its classical explainability.

Now, with these notations in place, we construct an ontological model for BCT as follows:

Definition 2.1

(An ontological model for BCT)
.

The ontological map
\tilde{\xi}:\text{BCT}\rightarrow\Delta
is the unique linear map specified by the following:

•

\tilde{\xi}
assigns to each system
n
an ontic space
\Lambda_{n}:=\tilde{\xi}{(n)}
, where for a non-trivial system
n\neq 1
, we define
\tilde{\xi}{(n)}
as classical system with the dimension
2n
, and for the trivial system
n=1
, we define
\tilde{\xi}{(n)}
to be the trivial system in classical theory as well, i.e.,
\tilde{\xi}{(n)}=1
. For non-trivial systems, this is depicted as

\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}
}\;.

(82)

•

Finally, we define the ontological model of BCT to be deterministic scalar-preserving, i.e., the ontological model maps scalar
1
in BCT to scalar
1
in classical theory, that is

\tilde{\xi}{(1)}:=1.

(83)

We have defined the ontological model on single system entities, namely pure states, pure effects, and normalised atomic transformations, as well as their multipartite counterparts. In App.
A
we will see how these two views are related, where as an example, in App.
D.2
, we use the results established in App.
A
to formalize reversible transformations of BCT in the ontological model.

2.1
Consistency checks

In this section, we aim to discuss whether the ontological model we have constructed for BCT is a consistent one. For an ontological model to be deemed consistent, as defined in
1.3
, it must be linear, diagram preserving, probability preserving (or empirically adequate), and determinacy preserving, ensuring that it maps instruments to valid instruments of classical theory, as we explain in the subsequent subsections and prove in App.
C
. What we have constructed as the ontological model of BCT is, by definition, a linear map whose action on systems, pure states, pure effects, normalised atomic transformations, and the scalar
1
has been explicitly defined. Hence, to determine whether the constructed ontological model is indeed consistent, we need to verify that it is consistent with linearity and that it satisfies diagram preservation, probability preservation, and determinacy preservation, all of which we will show to hold in what follows.

2.1.1
Linearity preservation

We have defined the ontological model to be linear, but a priori this could lead to inconsistencies. Namely, if we had two different linear decompositions of the same transformations in terms of normalised atomic transformations, then the ontological model could conceivably depend on which decomposition we used. This, however, is not a problem for BCT because all of the normalised atomic transformations are linearly independent, as we showed in Prop.
1.1
.

2.1.2
Diagram preservation

(85)

One also has both identity and swap preservation (
67
). When all of these conditions are satisfied, diagram preservation holds for every arbitrary scenario, such as (
66
).

The ontological model of BCT, as we have defined it, indeed satisfies diagram preservation, as we prove in App.
C.1
. In doing so, we first show that diagram preservation holds for the sequential composition of normalised atomic transformations. Then, using the linearity of the ontological model and the fact that every transformation is uniquely given as a conical combination of normalised atomic transformations (by Proposition
1.1
), we conclude that the model is diagram preserving for arbitrary sequential compositions.

For parallel composition, we reduce the preservation of an arbitrary pair of transformations to simpler conditions—including identity and swap preservation—whose joint satisfaction implies diagram preservation. These conditions are all fulfilled by virtue of Proposition
1.1
and the linearity of the ontological model.

Note that, for the sake of clarity, we have reviewed diagram preservation in Figures (
84
) and (
85
) only for the case where all systems are single and non-trivial. In App.
C.1
, we explain why diagram preservation also holds in other cases, not limited to this specific setting.

2.1.3
Probability preservation

Probability preservation follows directly from how the ontological model is defined on scalar
1
, i.e.,
\tilde{\xi}(1)=1
. Since any scalar
p\in[0,1]
can be expressed as
p.1
, probability preservation, and hence empirical adequacy, follows immediately from linearity of the ontological model, that is, for an arbitrary scalar
p\in[0,1]
, linearity implies
\tilde{\xi}(p)=\tilde{\xi}(p.1)=p\tilde{\xi}(1)=p
, which is pictorially represented as

2.1.4
Determinacy preservation

The ontological model must map every instrument in BCT to a valid instrument in classical theory. This requirement is satisfied, as demonstrated in App.
C.2
, where we prove that the ontological model preserves the unique deterministic effect. By diagram preservation, this implies that the ontological model maps every deterministic transformation in BCT to a deterministic transformation in classical theory—that is, a stochastic matrix. Consequently, instruments in BCT are mapped to valid instruments in classical theory. This follows because the full coarse-graining of an instrument is a deterministic transformation, and since the ontological model is linear and preserves determinacy, the full coarse-graining of the corresponding instrument in classical theory is also deterministic, ensuring its validity.

2.2
Bilocal classical theory admits an ontological model

We have shown that the model in Definition
2.1
satisfies all the requirements of Definition
1.3
, and so is a valid ontological model for BCT. Hence, we obtain the following result:

Theorem 2.2
.

There exists an ontological model for bilocal classical theory.

Thus, BCT is classically explainable and compatible with the notion of generalised noncontextuality, in the sense discussed in
[
62
,
73
]
. This might lead one to suspect that every locally-classical OPT admits of an ontological model and is hence classically explainable. However, as we show in the next section, this is not the case. To demonstrate this, we leverage the general OPT construction presented in Ref.
[
24
]
to build a specific counterexample: a locally-classical theory that violates local tomography and does not admit an ontological model.

3
A locally-classical theory that is not classically-explainable

3.1
Latent classical theories

Here, we aim to show that a class of locally-classical OPTs known as
latent classical theories
—obtained via the OPT construction introduced in Ref.
[
24
]
—unlike BCT, do not admit of any ontological model. This OPT construction was originally applied to quantum systems to define latent quantum theories (LQTs), namely, a family of OPTs that are locally quantum while violating local tomography.
3
3

3

“Locally quantum” here means that every system, be it elementary or composite, is quantum—while the composition postulate may generally differ from the standard quantum one. See also footnote
1
.
By applying the same construction to classical systems, one can similarly define the following:

Definition 3.1

(Latent classical theories (LCTs))
.

Latent classical theories
(LCTs) are the family of locally-classical OPTs defined by applying the construction of
[
24
, Apps. A-B]
to classical systems. Equivalently, LCTs may be defined as the restriction of LQTs
[
24
]
to their classical, namely, diagonal, sectors.

The key feature of LCTs is that they generally differ from standard classical theory in the composition rule. Intuitively, the composition rule for latent classical system is the usual one up to extra degrees of freedom “popping up” in the form of factor spaces. This generalises the standard classical composition rule. More concretely, for every pair of elementary latent classical systems
C_{1}
and
C_{2}
, there exists a classical space
L_{12}
such that

C_{1}C_{2}\coloneqq C_{1}\boxtimes C_{2}=L_{12}\otimes C_{1}\otimes C_{2}.

The space
L_{12}
is called the
latent factor
associated with the composite
C_{1}C_{2}
. Moreover, there exists a normalised state
\left|\kappa\right)_{L_{12}}
, called the
latent state
of
L_{12}
, such that the parallel composition of latent classical states reads as

\left|\sigma\right)_{C_{1}}\boxtimes\left|\tau\right)_{C_{2}}=\left|\kappa\right)_{L_{12}}\otimes\left|\sigma\right)_{C_{1}}\otimes\left|\tau\right)_{C_{2}}\quad\forall\left|\sigma\right)_{C_{1}}\in\textbf{St}(C_{1}),\left|\tau\right)_{C_{2}}\in\textbf{St}(C_{2}).

(87)

Therefore, whenever a LCT has a latent factor that is non-trivial—i.e., that is not one-dimensional—the resulting LCT will be different from standard classical theory. With this, we can prove the following result.

3.2
Latent classical theories do not admit ontological models

Theorem 3.2
.

There does not exist an ontological model for any latent classical theory where at least one latent state is not full-rank.

Proof.

Let us consider any LCT where there exists a pair of elementary latent classical systems
C_{1}
and
C_{2}
whose associated latent factor
L_{12}
has latent state
\left|\kappa\right)_{L_{12}}
that is not full-rank. Note that this implies that the associated latent factor
L_{12}
has dimension
d\geq 2
, meaning that the LCTs considered here are all different from standard classical theory. Therefore, by construction, there also exists at least one non-null effect
\left(\kappa^{\perp}\right|_{L_{12}}
such that
\left(\kappa^{\perp}|\kappa\right)_{L_{12}}=0
. Denoting the discarding of any system by
\left(\text{Tr}\right|
, we then define the composite effect
\left(b\right|_{C_{1}C_{2}}\coloneqq\left(\kappa^{\perp}\right|_{L_{12}}\otimes\left(\text{Tr}\right|_{C_{1}}\otimes\left(\text{Tr}\right|_{C_{2}}
that, in spite of being non-null, annihilates every product state in the light of Eq. (
87
), i.e.,

generalised Choi vector

\left|\gamma_{\text{Ch}}\right)_{SS}\coloneqq\sum_{i}|ii)_{SS}\in\textbf{St}_{\mathbb{R}}(SS)
and
a generalised Choi covector

\left(g_{\text{Ch}}\right|_{SS}\coloneqq\sum_{j}(jj|_{SS}\in\textbf{Eff}_{\mathbb{R}}(SS)
for every system
S

}\!\neq\ 0,

which is in contradiction with (

).
∎

Some comments are here in order. The above proof is based on more general techniques and results which will be presented in a forthcoming work
[
25
]
. In particular, by generalising the proof technique exploited here, Theorem
3.2
can be shown to hold even in the case where the image of the ontological model is taken to be an
infinite-dimensional classical theory
(provided that local tomography is satisfied)
[
25
]
. This means that the result is not an artifact of considering ontological models into a finite-dimensional classical theory. In fact, the LCTs that we defined in Theorem
3.2
cannot be embedded in any locally tomographic theory
[
25
]
. Remarkably, the example illustrated here is the first one (to our knowledge) of a theory exhibiting such a strong violation of local tomography, in the sense that it allows for the existence of a non-null bipartite effect annihilating every product state (as per Eq. (
88
)). By construction, the latter feature is common to LQTs
[
24
]
as well.

4
Conclusion

Figure 1:

Venn diagram incorporating our results. One example of a theory is included for each region, with the exception of a single region that is empty (since the only theory that is both locally tomographic and locally-classical is CT, which is, however, also classically-explainable). Our main results, Theorem
2.2
and Theorem
3.2
, allow us to populate the two regions of locally-classical theories which are non-locally tomographic.

The existence of an ontological model for BCT refutes the conjecture of Ref.
[
21
]
and shows that in general there is no tension between failures of local tomography and classical explainability (i.e., generalised noncontextuality). Indeed, the model constructed for BCT provides a way to locally account for non-locally tomographic degrees of freedom by locally adding extra ontic states. This matches with the results of Ref.
[
12
]
, and can in fact be viewed as the completion of the argument regarding holism from that work from a prepare-and-measure scenario to a fully compositional theory. Moreover, it embodies a concrete example that the assumption of local tomography used in the structure theorem in Ref.
[
62
]
is indeed a genuine limitation of the theorem.

Our proof technique for demonstrating the validity of the ontological model for BCT (see Appendices) provides a concrete methodology to define fully-fledged ontological models for other theories existing in the literature. The explicit model constructed here is also likely to provide a useful tool for further research into locally-classical theories. On the one hand, it provides a convenient diagrammatic representation of BCT which will be useful for better understanding the features of this theory. On the other hand, it provides a convenient route towards generalising this theory, both to further locally-classical theories, but also to general methods for modifying the composition rule of a given OPT. In particular, it opens the door to understanding the relationship between BCT and the
twirled
and
swirled

worlds
introduced in Refs.
[
12
,
85
]
.

We found that not every locally-classical theory is classically-explainable, as shown by the latent classical theories that we defined. Note that, for latent classical unipartite systems, every two-stage experiment where a state is prepared and a measurement is chosen out of a set of possible measurement settings (called a
prepare-and-measure scenario
) is clearly classically-explainable. In fact, latent classical unipartite systems satisfy a stronger property: since they are strictly classical (therefore simplicial), they are also
simplex-embeddable

[
65
]
by construction—and then, in particular, also
Kochen–Specker noncontextual

[
36
,
6
]
. Consequently, the failure to admit of an ontological model
[
62
]
is here due to how latent classical systems compose, essentially exhibiting a strong violation of local tomography—one that cannot be explained away due to the impossibility of embedding the theory into any locally tomographic one
[
25
]
. Note that this notion of classical explainability is sensitive to this kind of failure of nonclassicality, whereas the traditional Kochen–Specker
[
36
,
6
]
notion of noncontextuality is not, since the latter applies to single systems, whereas the generalised notion constrains all parts of a theory, including the theory’s composition rule. Hence, our results, that are summarised in Figure
1
, demonstrate that there is no straightforward relationship between theories being locally-classical and being classically-explainable. It would therefore be an interesting direction to find some physical principle which singles out which locally-classical theories are classically-explainable. This also underscores the fact that considering how systems compose is an important part of understanding what it means to be classical, just as it is an important part of defining and understanding any fully-fledged theory.

Appendix A
Relating single- and multi-system definitions

In the main text we define BCT and its ontological model using multi-system transformations, states, and effects. This was a choice for simplicity of presentation, and here we will show how to relate the single-system and multi-system definitions via explicit merging and splitting maps.

(94)

for all systems
n_{1}
,
n_{2}
, and for all
1\leq i\leq n_{1}
,
1\leq j\leq n_{2}
, and
s\in\{0,1\}
, where we define

Q(i,j,s):=2n_{1}(i-1)+(2j+s-1).

(95)

In other words,
\nu
maps each bipartite pure state with subsystems
n_{1}
and
n_{2}
to a pure state of a single system of size
2n_{1}n_{2}
. For each combination of
i
,
j
, and
s
, it assigns the pure state labeled by
Q(i,j,s)
, where
1\leq Q(i,j,s)\leq 2n_{1}n_{2}
.

In order to fully specify
\nu
we must specify its action on arbitrary multipartite pure states of any composite system in BCT, in particular we have that

(98)

results in the corresponding single-system pure state with the dimension
2^{p-1}n_{1}n_{2}n_{3}\ldots n_{p-1}n_{p}
, which we denote as
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\left[\rho\right]
. For example, for the cases of bipartite, tripartite and quadripartite pure states one has

\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{2}\left[(ij)_{s}\right]

\displaystyle=Q\left(i,j,s\right),

\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{3}\left[\big((ij)_{s}\,k\big)_{t}\right]

\displaystyle=Q\big(Q\left(i,j,s\right),k,t\big),

\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{4}\left[\Big(\big((ij)_{s}\,k\big)_{t}\,l\Big)_{u}\right]

\displaystyle=Q\Big(Q\big(Q\left(i,j,s\right),k,t\big),l,u\Big).

(99)

(102)

We can associate an effect
a_{l}
to the lower indices as

i_{1},i_{2},\cdots i_{p},s_{1},s_{2}\cdots,s_{p-1}\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;a_{l}=\left(\left(\cdots\left(\left(i_{1}i_{2}\right)_{s_{1}}i_{3}\right)_{s_{2}}\cdots i_{p-1}\right)_{s_{p-2}}i_{p}\right)_{s_{p-1}},

(103)

and a state
\rho_{u}
to the upper indices as

l_{1},l_{2},\cdots,l_{q},t_{1},t_{2}\cdots t_{q-1}\;\;\longrightarrow\;\;\rho_{u}=\left(\left(\cdots\left(\left(l_{1}l_{2}\right)_{t_{1}}l_{3}\right)_{t_{2}}\cdots l_{p-1}\right)_{t_{p-2}}l_{p}\right)_{t_{q-1}}.

a_{l}
and
\rho_{u}

A.2
In the ontological model

We map the splitting and merging transformations of BCT, namely
\nu
and its inverse as introduced in (
93
), (
94
), and (
96
), to define splittings and mergings for the ontological model, namely
\mu
and its inverse

) can be verified when we apply both sides to the orthonormal basis of the corresponding classical space. Similarly, for

(115)

Having defined
\nu
and consequently
\mu
, we can alternatively define the ontological model only for single-system entities, namely, single-system pure states, single-system pure effects, and single-system normalised atomic transformations. This, in turn, enables us to derive their multipartite counterparts, which we will show to be consistent with the direct definitions we have given for multipartite entities in the ontological model.

94
). If we apply the ontological model on the both sides, we have

), and then applying
\mu
, as shown in the middle diagram. This confirms that diagram preservation holds in this instance.

The first diagram corresponds to the use of the ontological model, regardless of whether or not the model satisfies diagram preservation. This is equal to the final diagram—i.e., when the ontological model is used on the pure state resulting from the action of
\nu
. On the other hand, according to our definition of the ontological model on a pure composite states in (
78
), one can show that in the case where diagram preservation holds—as in the second diagram in the equation above—if one first applies the ontological model to the original composite pure state, and then applies
\mu
, the result will match that of the last diagram. Therefore, diagram preservation holds in this specific instance, and by recursively applying this reasoning, one can derive (
119
). The same argument applies to a composite pure effect in equation (
120
), where using what we define in (
80
) one can show that diagram diagram preservation holds when one has

(129)

To show why a transformation
\mathscr{A}
on composite systems is atomic if and only if (
B
) holds, recall (
A.1
) (originally stated for normalised atomic transformations, but it can be straightforwardly extended to atomic transformations by multiplying both sides by a scalar factor
\lambda
, which does not affect the argument). In this setting,
\mathscr{A}
is expressed in terms of an atomic transformation
\mathscr{A}_{s}
on the corresponding single system, and for clarity we denote this as
\mathscr{A}=\nu_{p}\circ\mathscr{A}_{s}\circ\nu^{-1}_{q}
, where
\nu_{p}
denotes the consecutive application of
\nu
for
p
times, and
\nu^{-1}_{q}
denotes the consecutive application of
\nu^{-1}
for
q
times.

To prove that
\mathscr{A}
is atomic if and only if it satisfies (
B
), is equivalent of proving,
\mathscr{A}
is atomic if and only if
\mathscr{A}_{s}
is atomic. To see this equivalence, consider a transformation
\mathscr{A}
on a composite system that satisfies (
B
), without assuming atomicity. Then, by (
B
), there exists a single-system transformation
\mathscr{A}_{s}
such that
\mathscr{A}
can be expressed in terms of
\mathscr{A}_{s}
as
\mathscr{A}=\nu_{p}\circ\mathscr{A}_{s}\circ\nu^{-1}_{q}
. Since
\mathscr{A}_{s}
satisfies (
47
), it is atomic. Therefore, to conclude that
\mathscr{A}
is atomic, it suffices to show that the atomicity of
\mathscr{A}_{s}
implies the atomicity of
\mathscr{A}
. Also, to show the other direction, that an atomic transformation
\mathscr{A}
satisfies (
B
), we can define a transformation
\mathscr{A}_{s}
such that one can rewrite
\mathscr{A}
in terms of
\mathscr{A}_{s}
as
\mathscr{A}=\nu_{p}\circ\mathscr{A}_{s}\circ\nu^{-1}_{q}
. If we can show that the atomicity of
\mathscr{A}
implies the atomicity of
\mathscr{A}_{s}
, then it follows that
\mathscr{A}_{s}
satisfies (
47
), which ultimately implies that
\mathscr{A}
satisfies (
B
). Hence, to prove that
\mathscr{A}
is atomic if and only if it satisfies (
B
), one must prove
\mathscr{A}
is atomic if and only if
\mathscr{A}_{s}
is atomic.

This indeed follows from the properties of
\nu
. We can use proof by contradiction to show that the atomicity of
\mathscr{A}_{s}
implies the atomicity of
\mathscr{A}
. For that, suppose
\mathscr{A}_{s}
is atomic, but
\mathscr{A}
is not. This means there exist two transformations
\mathscr{A}_{1}
and
\mathscr{A}_{2}
such that
\mathscr{A}=\mathscr{A}_{1}+\mathscr{A}_{2}
and
\mathscr{A}_{1}\not\propto\mathscr{A}_{2}
. But this leads to contradiction, since one has
\mathscr{A}_{s}=\nu^{-1}_{q}\circ\mathscr{A}_{1}\circ\nu_{p}+\nu^{-1}_{q}\circ\mathscr{A}_{2}\circ\nu_{p}
, and using the properties of
\nu
implies that
\mathscr{A}_{s}
is not atomic, because
\nu^{-1}_{q}\circ\mathscr{A}_{1}\circ\nu_{p}\not\propto\nu^{-1}_{q}\circ\mathscr{A}_{2}\circ\nu_{p}
. Hence,
\mathscr{A}
is atomic. The same logic can be applied to show the other direction. That is, the atomicity of
\mathscr{A}
implies the atomicity of
\mathscr{A}_{s}
. If one assumes the contrary, that is
\mathscr{A}_{s}
is not atomic, then one would be led to a contradiction of having
\mathscr{A}
as a non atomic transformation. Therefore,
\mathscr{A}
is atomic if and only if
\mathscr{A}_{s}
is atomic. Moreover, one can show that every transformation
t
on composite systems can be uniquely expressed as a conical combination of atomic transformations on composite systems. This follows directly from Proposition
1.1
, since any transformation on composite systems can be mapped to a transformation on single systems via
\nu
. Consequently, one obtains a unique conical combination of atomic transformations
\mathscr{A}_{s}
on single systems, which in turn implies that the conical combination of the corresponding composite normalised atomic transformations
\mathscr{A}
is also unique for the original transformation.

\mu
in the form it appears in (
A.2
), along with the above result, ensures that diagram preservation holds for the sequential composition of atomic transformations when systems are composite. Hence, diagram preservation also holds for the sequential composition of arbitrary transformations when systems are composite.

(151)

Hence, the ontological model is swapping preserving. Swapping preservation, together with (
145
), implies that (
134
) holds. Therefore, the ontological model is diagram preserving for the parallel composition of arbitrary transformations. Similarly, using
\mu
the way it has been used in (
A.2
), one can show that diagram preservation also holds for the parallel composition of arbitrary transformations when systems are composite.

Note that here we have only shown diagram preservation in the case where every system, whether a single system or a composite system, is non-trivial. Nevertheless, since our ontological model defines how pure states, pure effects, normalised atomic transformations, and scalar
1
are mapped, one can use the same reasoning to show that diagram preservation also holds when at least one system is trivial. In other words, in such cases, it is possible to breakdown an arbitrary composition into a conical combination of normalised atomic transformations, pure effects, pure states, and scalar
1
. Then, by the linearity of the ontological model, one can verify diagram preservation for arbitrary compositions involving at least one trivial system.

(155)

which holds true for transformations involving composite systems as well. This ensures that the ontological model maps every arbitrary instrument in BCT to a valid instrument in classical theory. This follows from coarse-graining preservation. Since the full coarse-graining of all transformations within a given instrument yields a deterministic transformation, linearity of the ontological model and determinacy preservation imply that the coarse-graining of the corresponding transformations in classical theory is also deterministic. Therefore, the corresponding instrument in classical theory is itself a valid instrument.

Appendix D
Reversible transformations

D.1
In bilocal classical theory

For all systems
n\neq 1
, a transformation
\mathscr{R}
is reversible in BCT if and only if, there exists a permutation
\pi
of
n
elements and a binary variable
\sigma_{i}\in\{0,1\}
, such that for all non-trivial ancillary systems
E
, and all bipartite pure states
|(ij)_{s})
of the system of interest and ancilla, one has

D.2
In the ontological model

Here we derive the ontological representation of reversible transformations in BCT. This is not strictly necessary for any of our results, but shows example calculations that can be performed using the ontological representation, and provides a tool which will be useful for future research on applications of BCT.

(164)

where
\sigma_{Q(i,j,s)}\in\{0,1\}
, and
\pi\left(Q\left(i,j,s\right)\right)
denotes a permutation of
2nm
elements. Note that we have assumed that if a reversible transformation
\mathscr{R}
on bipartite systems can be expressed in terms of a transformation
\mathscr{R}_{s}
on the corresponding single system as
\mathscr{R}=\nu\circ\mathscr{R}_{s}\circ\nu^{-1}
, then
\mathscr{R}_{s}
is reversible itself, where we used the reversibility of
\mathscr{R}_{s}
in the last equality of the equation above. This indeed holds, as the existence of the inverse of
\mathscr{R}
implies that its corresponding single-system transformation is the inverse of
\mathscr{R}_{s}
. Therefore,
\mathscr{R}_{s}
is indeed reversible.

\pi\left(Q\left(i,j,s\right)\right)
is also representing a permutation of a bipartite pure state, we define

(165)

In other words, the permuted bipartite pure state corresponding to the permuted single pure state
\pi(Q(i,j,s))
can be denoted as
|(i^{\prime}j^{\prime})_{s^{\prime}})
, where one has
1\leq i^{\prime}\leq n
,
1\leq j^{\prime}\leq m
, and
s^{\prime}\in\{0,1\}
, each being a function of the original indices of the bipartite state, which we denote this functional relation as
i^{\prime}=\pi_{n}(i,j,s)
,
j^{\prime}=\pi_{m}(i,j,s)
, and
s^{\prime}=\pi_{B}(i,j,s)
. Therefore, one has

(169)

Alternatively, we can express any reversible transformation on bipartite systems as a conical combination of normalised atomic transformations on bipartite systems. By determining the explicit form of the conical coefficients and applying the ontological model, one derives the same result as in (
D.2
).
